title: The servant's ear (Luke 22:47–53)
hookLine: even while arrested he heals the ear Peter cut off

cards: The prayer in the garden is over. Torches come up the hill: a crowd with swords and clubs, and at the front a familiar face, Judas, one of the twelve, leaning in to kiss his teacher. In the dark it happens fast.
Someone near Jesus asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? and doesn't wait for the answer. A blade swings. The servant of the high priest is holding the side of his head; his right ear is gone.
What Jesus does next is the last healing Luke records before the cross.

teach.b: All four Gospels tell of the sword in the garden. Only John gives the names: the one with the sword is Simon Peter, and the servant is Malchus.
Only Luke, the doctor's Gospel by old tradition, tells what happened next: "But Jesus answering, said: Suffer ye thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him."
Suffer ye thus far is an old phrase, and nobody is fully sure of the Greek's exact sense. Many modern readers hear no more of this: enough, stop here.
Others hear Jesus speaking to the crowd: let me go this far, let me reach him. Either way, the fighting ends with a hand on a stranger's wound.

teach.h: HE HEALS THE MAN WHO CAME FOR HIM.
teach.b: Look who gets healed: not a friend or a disciple, but a man who came out at night to arrest him. And look when: Jesus is about to be bound, and his own hands are still free to touch.

Then he tells the chief priests and captains plainly that they could have taken him any day in the temple, "but this is your hour, and the power of darkness." He names the darkness and doesn't fight it with a sword.
He refuses violence, and he repairs what his own side broke.

teach.h: HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.
teach.b: Peter swung the blade; Jesus cleans up after Peter. Most of the damage we have to mend wasn't done by our enemies. It was done by us, or by people on our side, trying to help.

how: Catholics hear the arrest in the garden in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and the healing of the servant's ear is preached by many as Christ's refusal of violence even in his own defense.

games.q: you're Jesus. the crowd has come for you, one of yours has just cut off a servant's ear, and everyone is waiting to see if this becomes a fight. what do you do?
o: tell your friends to fight while you get away.
stop it, and heal the servant's ear.
say nothing and let it play out.
games.why: "Suffer ye thus far." he touches the ear and heals it, then lets himself be taken. the last healing before the cross goes to one of the men who came for him.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that broke because of you: a sharp word in a group chat, a borrowed thing returned worse, a friendship you let go quiet on purpose.

Picture what touching it would look like: a message, an apology with no excuse attached, fixing the thing. If you pray, ask for the nerve to mend it; if not, just hold it in front of you and choose one small next step.

wordCard.voice: Malchus. The name John gives the servant whose ear Peter cut off, and whom Jesus touched and healed while the soldiers closed in. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: ear, the word Luke uses when Jesus touches it. (Luke 22:51)

carryVoice: Your line: no more of this. A hand on a wound, right where a fight was starting. That's day four hundred eighty-two.
